messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 73
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Journalist
- Trauma Type: Man-made disaster
- Pcl5: 74

# The Weight of What He Witnessed

Martin is a 73-year-old retired journalist who spent four decades covering stories across North America, building a reputation for being the man who showed up when no one else wanted to. He is divorced, lives alone in a small apartment in Chicago, and still keeps a battered press badge pinned to the corkboard above his desk — a habit he cannot bring himself to break. He came to therapy reluctantly, referred by his physician after a series of what he called "bad patches" that had begun interfering with his sleep, his eating, and what little social life he had maintained since his marriage ended twelve years ago.

The event that changed Martin occurred eleven years ago, when he was assigned to cover the aftermath of a large industrial chemical explosion at a manufacturing plant outside Cleveland. He arrived within hours of the blast, credentialed and experienced, certain that this was simply another story. What he found was not simply another story. Several workers had been trapped inside a secondary structure that collapsed after the initial explosion, and Martin was standing close enough to the perimeter fence to hear men screaming inside the smoke. Emergency responders were delayed by a second, smaller explosion. Martin watched through a chain-link fence for nearly forty minutes as rescue workers were held back and three men died within what felt like arm's reach of help. He photographed it. He filed the story. He won a regional award for his coverage. He told himself, as he had always told himself, that bearing witness was the job.

He did not fall apart immediately. For several years he continued working, filed more stories, covered more difficult scenes. But something had shifted in the architecture of how he moved through the world. He began avoiding assignments that involved industrial sites or large crowds. He told his editor it was a question of interest, not capacity. His marriage, already strained by decades of emotional distance, ended the year after the explosion, though Martin connects the two events only reluctantly.

Now, in retirement, the distance he once maintained through constant motion has collapsed. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with his heart hammering, having dreamed some version of that fence, those sounds, that smoke. During the day, certain triggers — the chemical smell of cleaning products, the wail of a distant siren, footage of industrial accidents on the television news — can drop him back into the scene with a vividness that startles him. He describes standing in his kitchen one morning, smelling a neighbor's gas stove through the ventilation, and finding himself gripping the counter, unable to move, certain for a long moment that he was back at that fence.

Martin describes a persistent, bone-deep sense that he did something wrong that day, though he is intellectually unable to articulate what he could have done differently. He was not a rescue worker. He had no equipment. He knows this. The knowing does not help. He carries a quiet conviction that his presence — his watching, his photographing — was a form of participation in something shameful, and this belief has calcified into a general sense that he is not a person who deserves ease or comfort.

He has become largely isolated. He declines invitations from former colleagues, keeps phone calls short, and fills his days with solitary routines: coffee, newspapers, long walks along the lakefront that he describes as the only time he feels something close to neutral. He has stopped writing entirely, which he describes as the most disorienting loss of all — writing was always the way he processed the world, and now the blank page feels like an accusation.

He sits across from his therapist with the careful posture of a man who has spent a lifetime presenting composure as competence, and says, with a dry, practiced humor that does not quite reach his eyes, that he supposes he has been filing the wrong kind of stories for a very long time.
